chapter: Steely Dan and L.A. session life
title: Writing horn arrangements for Steely Dan's Aja album
summary: Walter Becker called him to write horn parts; he describes the brief and the players hired.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: At what point in Steely Dan recordings did you get the tunes that you were going to add horn section parts to?

Right. Well I had met Walter Becker, one half of Steely Dan of course, through a mutual friend. And so I got a call from him saying, “Look we are working on our new album” [Steely Dan] and I wondered if you could come down and listen and maybe write some horn arrangements.” I was like great. Because Steely Dan was already, you know, a very hot property. So I walked into Village Recorders in West Los Angeles and I met Donald Fagan and their producer — I can’t think of his name right now. Donald and Walter led the proceedings. So they played me the tunes. They told me, here’s what they said: “We want a lot of horns” you know he says, “but we don’t want any like high screaming trumpet parts.” I said okay, I won’t write high screaming trumpet parts. But we ended up with, we agreed on a section that was I think four saxes, two trombones, two trumpets I think that’s what it turned out to be. So they gave me a reel to reel tape in those days of course of the tunes except for Aja of course, which is the tune that has the Wayne Shorter solo and didn’t require any horn sweetening. So I go home and I began to write. And we had set up sessions, I heard the band, which included let’s see I think Pete couldn’t do it because they were night sessions and he was doing “The Tonight Show” at the time. But
I got Plas Johnson; Jackie Kelso, another wonderful saxophone player; Bill Perkins, another saxophone player.
Jim Horn was on it too? Oh my gosh okay.
I’m sure it’s right if you say so. And Chuck Findley and somebody else on trumpet, I don’t remember who. And Slyde Hyde and somebody else, maybe Lew McCreary on trumpet — on trombone I mean.
